title: Blandina of Lyon (177)
hookLine: an enslaved woman outlasts her torturers with one short answer

lines: HER OWNER WAS AFRAID FOR HER.
cards: Her owner was afraid for her. That's where her part of the story begins. Persecution has broken out in Lyon, a city in Gaul, and Christians are being dragged before the crowd.
Among them are Blandina, who is enslaved, and the woman who owns her. The other Christians are afraid for her too. Her body seems weak, and they fear she won't even manage to say what she believes.
The letter that tells this story was written by the Christians of Lyon and Vienne, and it has a surprise in it. The one they worried about becomes the one the letter dwells on.

teach.b: Eusebius, the Church historian, copied the letter into his history, so it can still be read. First, the doubt. Blandina's own people expect her to break.
Second, the torturers give up. The letter says they took turns on her from morning until evening, until they were worn out themselves. They admitted they were beaten.
They had nothing more to do to her, and were amazed she was still breathing. Third, her answer.

teach.h: THE SAME ANSWER, OVER AND OVER.
teach.b: The charge hanging over the Christians is the old slander that they do terrible things in secret, the same rumors Justin was answering yesterday. Her answer, in Greek: Christianē eimi. Christian, I am.
And among us, nothing evil is done. The letter says saying it gave her strength again, and rest, and took away the pain. The answer wasn't a speech.

It was a name, and she held to it. Fourth, the stake. Later she's hung on a stake in the arena, and the letter says the others, looking at her stretched out there, saw in their sister the one who was crucified for them.
An enslaved woman became the picture of Christ for those suffering with her.
The Church still remembers the martyrs of Lyon together, and Blandina's name stands beside her bishop's. It's a story about courage, and also about who gets underestimated.
The one nobody expected to stand turned out to be holding everyone else up.

how: Catholics remember the martyrs of Lyon, Saint Pothinus the bishop, Saint Blandina and their companions, together in the Church's calendar of saints, and their story is read from the letter Eusebius preserved.

o: Greek for Christ is risen, an Easter greeting
Greek for Christian, I am: Blandina's answer
Latin for I believe, the first words of a creed

games.q: Blandina of Lyon — tap the pairs.
p: the city in Gaul where it happened
worn out from morning to evening
the others saw Christ in her

s: the letter says she was enslaved; the woman who owned her was arrested too.
the letter says her torturers gave up before she did
they took turns from morning to evening, then admitted they were beaten.
the letter says she stayed silent the whole time
she answered: Christian, and nothing evil is done among us.

games.q: you're Blandina. the crowd believes Christians do terrible things in secret, and the torture goes on. what do you say?
o: whatever they want, to stop the pain.
Christian, and nothing evil is done among us.
games.why: the letter gives that short answer, and says that saying it gave her strength again.

practice: Blandina's answer was short, and she held to it.

Look for one small thing in your life that bends too easily, an honest answer you tend to blur, a promise you keep postponing, and picture yourself holding steady, without a speech, just the same quiet answer.
If you pray, ask God for a little of her steadiness.

wordCard.voice: Christianē eimi. Greek for Christian, I am: Blandina's short answer, repeated until it gave her strength again. Today's word.
